name: Question 2
problem:
Consider the following inexact differential equation.

$$
{x}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x=0
$$

Select the correct options in the reasoning below about whether $I(y)=\frac{1}{y}$ is an integrating factor of this equation.

To show that $I(y)=\frac{1}{y}$ is an integrating factor for the given differential equation, we need to check if the following equation is exact:

$$
{{field-1}}=0
$$

For this equation, let's denote

$$
P=-y,\,Q=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.
$$

So, the corresponding partial derivatives are

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\,{{field-2}},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\,{{field-3}}.
$$

Now, since 

$$
{{field-4}},
$$

the transformed equation {{field-5}} exact.

Therefore, $I(y)=\frac{1}{y}$ {{field-6}} an integrating factor for the initial differential equation.
worked_solution:
A function $I(x,y)$ is an integrating factor for the differential equation

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0,
$$

if the following equation is exact:

$$
I(x,y)[P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y]=0.
$$

In our case, we need to check if the following equation is exact:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y}({x}^{2}\,\text{d}y-{y}^{2}\,\text{d}x) & =0 \\ -y\,\text{d}x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\text{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\text{d}y=0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\frac{∂Q}{∂x}.
$$

For our transformed equation, we have  

$$
P(x,y)=-y,\,Q(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}}{y}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-y)=-1 \\ \frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{{x}^{2}}{y})=\frac{2x}{y}\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}\ne \frac{∂Q}{∂x},
$$

the transformed equation $\text{isn't}$ exact.

Therefore, $I(y)=\frac{1}{y}$ $\text{isn't}$ an integrating factor for the initial differential equation.

EXPLANATION

A function I(x,y) is an integrating factor for the differential equation P(x,y)dx+Q(x,y)dy=0, if the following equation is exact: I(x,y)[P(x,y)dx+Q(x,y)dy]=0.

In our case, we need to check if the following equation is exact:

1y(x2dy−y2dx)=0−ydx+x2ydy=0

Recall that a differential equation of the form

P(x,y)dx+Q(x,y)dy=0

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

∂P∂y=∂Q∂x.

For our transformed equation, we have

P(x,y)=−y,Q(x,y)=x2y.

Now, we compute the partial derivatives: ∂P∂y=∂∂y(−y)=−1∂Q∂x=∂∂x(x2y)=2xy

Since ∂P∂y≠∂Q∂x, the transformed equation isn't exact.

Therefore, I(y)=1y isn't an integrating factor for the initial differential equation.
